import pandas as pd,numpy as np,statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('ab_test.csv');print(d.shape,d.isna().sum().sum(),d.user_id.duplicated().sum())
i=d[d.platform=='ios'].copy();i['t']=(i.variant=='treatment').astype(int)
print(len(i),i.groupby('variant').converted.agg(['mean','size']))
rows=[]
for c,g in i.groupby('country'):
    a=g[g.t==1].converted;b=g[g.t==0].converted
    dl=a.mean()-b.mean();se=np.sqrt(a.var()/len(a)+b.var()/len(b))
    rows.append((c,len(b),len(a),b.mean(),a.mean(),dl,dl-1.96*se,dl+1.96*se))
r=pd.DataFrame(rows,columns='c nc nt pc pt d lo hi'.split());print(r.round(4))
tot=(r.d*(r.nc+r.nt)).sum()
print(smf.logit('converted~t',i).fit(disp=0).params)
m0=smf.logit('converted~t+C(country)',i).fit(disp=0);m1=smf.logit('converted~t*C(country)',i).fit(disp=0)
from scipy import stats
lr=2*(m1.llf-m0.llf);print('LR p',stats.chi2.sf(lr,4))
# all-country x variant within platform share
print(d.groupby(['platform','country']).size().unstack())
# contribution
r['contrib']=r.d*(r.nt)/r.nt.sum();print(r[['c','contrib']],r.contrib.sum())
# permutation-ish: heterogeneity via Q
w=1/((r.hi-r.lo)/3.92)**2;pm=(w*r.d).sum()/w.sum();Q=(w*(r.d-pm)**2).sum();print('Q p',stats.chi2.sf(Q,4))
# full table all platforms
for p,g in d.groupby('platform'):
  print(p,g.groupby(['country','variant']).converted.mean().unstack().assign(d=lambda x:x.treatment-x.control).round(3).d.to_dict())

events.text:
The iOS lift is largest in Germany (DE) and India (IN), but the data can't show that it differs by country. The country differences could be noise, because each country has only about 250 iOS users per arm.

| iOS country | n per arm (control / treatment) | Control | Treatment | Lift (pp) | 95% CI | Share of iOS lift |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DE | 286 / 257 | 8.0% | 17.5% | **+9.5** | [3.8, 15.1] | 46% |
| IN | 239 / 306 | 8.4% | 14.4% | **+6.0** | [0.7, 11.3] | 35% |
| BR | 258 / 278 | 9.3% | 12.2% | +2.9 | [-2.3, 8.2] | 15% |
| UK | 280 / 250 | 11.4% | 12.0% | +0.6 | [-4.9, 6.1] | 3% |
| US | 268 / 240 | 11.9% | 12.1% | +0.1 | [-5.5, 5.8] | 1% |
| **iOS overall** | 1331 / 1331 | 9.8% | 13.7% | **+3.8** | [1.4, 6.3] | 100% |

- **Concentration:** DE and IN account for about 81% of the iOS lift. The US and UK are near zero, but their intervals still allow gains of about 5pp.
- **Same everywhere?** Not shown either way. The test for whether the lift differs by country gives p=0.11 (likelihood-ratio test; a Cochran Q test gives the same). The data can't reject a uniform lift of about 4pp.
- **Strength of evidence by country:** Only DE holds up after correcting for the 5 country tests (p≈0.001). IN (p≈0.03) does not.

Caveats:
- **IN assignment looks unbalanced.** IN on iOS has 239 control against 306 treatment users (p=0.004). After correcting for 15 platform-by-country cells, p≈0.06. The overall split is fine (p=0.59), but the IN lift may be biased by how users were assigned or logged. Check that before relying on IN.
- **Post-hoc segment.** I picked iOS after seeing it was the winner (its own platform-interaction p=0.064), so all of this is exploratory.
- **DE is not a country-wide effect.** DE Android is -3.9pp, so the DE gain looks specific to iOS.
- **Whole-test context:** the overall lift is +1.66pp (p=0.025), and Android is slightly negative.
- **Data checks:** The data has no nulls or duplicates. These were checked in an earlier session and re-confirmed.

I used the first rows from my saved notes rather than re-printing sample rows, because the data wasn't new to me. The notes in `/memories/ab_test.md` are updated with these results.

## Findings
- Conversion 8.21% ctrl vs 9.87% treat: +1.66pp [0.21, 3.11], +20% rel, p=0.025. Adjusted (variant+platform+country) OR ~1.2, p~0.03.
- By platform: iOS +3.8pp [1.4, 6.3]; web +1.1pp [-1.5, 3.6]; Android -0.7pp [-3.0, 1.5]. Interaction p=0.064. Country interaction p=0.36 (none).
